questions.question:
**A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate option. Choose the correct alternative.**

The storm passed ________ but the night remained warm.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Option 3 - quickly**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence requires an adverb to describe how the storm passed.
 
• We use adverbs to add more information about a verb, an adjective, another adverb, a clause, or a whole sentence.
 
• "**Quickly**" is the appropriate adverb as it describes **the speed** at which the storm passed.
 
• The use of comparative forms such as "quicker" or "quickest" would be incorrect as there is no comparison being made.
 
• "Quick" is an adjective and does not fit grammatically in the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is **option 3**.

**Complete sentence:** *The storm passed quickly __but the night remained warm.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• Option 1 - "**quickest**" is a superlative form of the adjective "quick" and cannot be used as an adverb.
 
• Option 2 - "**quicker**" is a comparative form of the adjective "quick" and cannot be used as an adverb without the suffix "**-ly**".
 
• Option 4 - "**quick**" is an adjective and cannot be used to describe how the storm passed.

questions.question:
**Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.**

Before he could devote many more / thought to the matter, Pranav / had stepped up to him.

options.text: Before he could devote many more

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: "**Before he could devote many more.**"

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The error lies in the first segment of the sentence.
 
• The phrase "**many more**" is not grammatically correct in this context.
 
• It should be "**much more**" instead.
 
• "**Many more**" is used when referring to countable objects or things that can be enumerated. It is used to emphasize a larger number or quantity of items.
 
 
• **For example-** *After the sale, there were many more people in the store than before.*
 
 
 
• "**Much more**" is used when referring to uncountable or non-specific quantities, such as abstract concepts or substances that can't be easily counted.
 
 
• **For example-** *She needs much more patience to complete this project.*
 
 
 
• *​*The word "**thought**" is being quantified in the given sentence, and since "**thought**" refers to an abstract concept that cannot be counted, "**much more**" is the appropriate phrase to use.

Therefore, the correct answer is **option 1**.

**The sentence should read:** *Before he could devote much more thought to the matter, Pranav had stepped up to him.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2**: The name "**Pranav**" is correctly placed in the sentence.
 
• **Option 3**: The verb "**had stepped up**" is also correctly used in the sentence.
